title: Kumbhakarna
hook: Ravana loses his first duel, and orders the giant who sleeps for months to be woken

segments.voice: Yesterday: the serpent-arrows and Garuda, and the old story behind them: two sisters, a cheat, a son who freed his mother. Did you thank someone loyal? A new week begins, and Ravana himself goes out to fight. Day six hundred forty-five.

Ravana finally rides out himself. He strikes Lakshmana down with a great dart and tries to lift him to carry him off, and can't move him. Hanuman can, easily, and carries Lakshmana to safety. Then Rama meets Ravana, smashes his chariot, and cuts the crown from his head. And Rama stops. You've fought hard today, he says, and you're tired. Go home. Rest. Come back tomorrow, and see what I can do. Ravana goes home, alive, beaten, humiliated. And he gives an order: wake my brother.
screen: `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `GO HOME AND REST.` → `WAKE MY BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Ravana's brother is Kumbhakarna, and his name says it: pot-ears. He's a giant beyond giants, and he sleeps. Not for a night. For months. Waking him is a comic set-piece in the war book, and Valmiki enjoys it. Rakshasas pile up mountains of food beside him, meat and rice and great jars to drink. They beat drums and blow conches by his ears. They shout. They hit him with clubs and hammers. They march elephants over his body. Nothing. Finally, after all that, he yawns, stretches, and wakes up hungry. Why does he sleep like that? Valmiki gives two answers in different places. In the Yuddha Kanda, Vibhishana tells Rama that when Kumbhakarna was young he devoured creatures without limit, and Brahma, the creator, cursed him to sleep as if dead. Ravana begged for mercy, so Brahma softened it: he'd sleep for six months and wake for a single day. In the Uttara Kanda the story goes differently. When Kumbhakarna was about to ask Brahma for a boon, the gods were afraid of what he'd ask, so the goddess Sarasvati entered his speech, and the boon he asked for was sleep. Later tellers added a pun: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, indrasana, and the word came out nidrasana, the seat of sleep. Notice the shape of this. Ravana is now pinning his hopes on someone he has left asleep through the war so far. A giant piece on his board, and he only reaches for it when he's losing.
screen: `KUMBHAKARNA: POT-EARS.` · `DRUMS, CLUBS AND ELEPHANTS.` · `A CURSE, OR A TWISTED BOON.` · `INDRASANA BECOMES NIDRASANA.` · then, large: `WOKEN ONLY WHEN RAVANA IS LOSING.`

segments.voice: Sit and let yourself be heavy, like a sleeper. Feel the weight of the body in the chair or on the floor. Now ask: what in me is asleep that I only wake when things go wrong? A strength, a friendship, a habit, a gift. Don't bang drums at it. Just notice it, gently, the way you'd look in on someone sleeping. Breathe in, and let it stir. The bell holds the time.
Kumbhakarna. Ravana's giant brother, pot-ears, who sleeps for months under a curse or a twisted boon, woken only now that Ravana is losing.
Your line: Kumbhakarna. Today, wake one strength you only call on in emergencies, and use it on an ordinary task. Day six hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: The waking of Kumbhakarna is a favorite scene in Ramlila and in shadow-puppet traditions, often played for laughs before his serious conversation with Ravana.

fork.setup: you're Rama. Ravana's chariot is smashed and his crown is cut away. he's exhausted in front of you. what do you do?
options: send him home to rest and come back tomorrow.
fork.reveal: Rama tells him he's tired, to go home and rest, and return to see Rama's strength.

original.note: Sanskrit Kumbhakarṇa: from kumbha, pot or jar, and karṇa, ear.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kumbhakarna is just a lazy giant.
what it means: his sleep is a curse from Brahma, or a boon twisted by Sarasvati, depending on which book of Valmiki you read.
what a scholar hears: the indrasana–nidrasana pun is a later teller's wordplay; Valmiki's Uttara Kanda simply has him ask for sleep.
